claim: Class 9 (2026) teaches that the south-west monsoon is 'mainly caused by the unequal heating of land and the sea': land warms faster, low pressure over the subcontinent, cooler Indian Ocean has high pressure, moist winds blow to land
source: NCERT Grade 9 Understanding Society: India and Beyond Part 1, Ch3 (first ed. June 2026)
note: This records what NCERT Grade 9 says. The chapter does not mention the ITCZ, jet streams, ENSO or the Himalaya's role in the monsoon (word search). Audit D3 fix, 2 Nov 2026.

claim: NCERT Class XI: differential heating of land and sea creates seasonal pressure zones whose differences reverse monsoon winds; but p.30 adds that no single theory has fully explained the monsoon and a breakthrough came when it was studied at the global rather than regional level
value: land-sea heating plus an admission of incompleteness
source: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch4 Climate (rev. ed. Feb 2022, reprint Mar 2026)
note: The Class XI text itself gives the simple view and says it is incomplete.

claim: NCERT Class XI treats land and sea breezes as a daily local wind: land heats faster by day so air rises, pressure gradient sea to land; reverses at night
source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch9 (rationalised ed. Dec 2022, reprint 2026-27)
second_source: NCERT Grade 9 Understanding Society: India and Beyond Part 1, Ch3 (first ed. June 2026)
note: Same book (p.80) says the monsoon is the most pronounced effect of seasonal shifting of heating and pressure belts, and sends the reader to India: Physical Environment.

claim: Sea heats and cools slowly, land quickly (specific heat idea behind the land-sea contrast)
source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch8 (rationalised ed. Dec 2022, reprint 2026-27)

claim: Halley (1686) proposed that the primary cause of the monsoon was differential heating of ocean and land, a gigantic land-sea breeze; some scientists still treat it as the basic mechanism
source: Gadgil S. (2003) The Indian monsoon and its variability. Annu. Rev. Earth Planet. Sci. 31:429-467 (doi 10.1146/annurev.earth.31.100901.141251)
second_source: Geen, Bordoni, Battisti, Hui (2020) Monsoons, ITCZs, and the concept of the global monsoon. Rev. Geophys. 58, e2020RG000700

claim: Simpson (1921) argued the observations do not fit the land-sea breeze view: India is hotter in May than in July, the hottest part (north-west) gets no monsoon rain, and average temperature is higher in bad-rain years
value: three observations against the sea-breeze idea
source: Gadgil S. (2003) The Indian monsoon and its variability. Annu. Rev. Earth Planet. Sci. 31:429-467 (doi 10.1146/annurev.earth.31.100901.141251)
second_source: Geen, Bordoni, Battisti, Hui (2020) Monsoons, ITCZs, and the concept of the global monsoon. Rev. Geophys. 58, e2020RG000700
note: Paraphrased; Gadgil quotes Simpson at length.

claim: Over 1950-2014 the June-September land surface temperature over India was negatively correlated with all-India monsoon rainfall (r = -0.38), and stronger monsoons went with a weaker, not stronger, land-ocean contrast
source: Gadgil S. (2018) The monsoon system: Land-sea breeze or the ITCZ? J. Earth Syst. Sci. 127:1 (doi 10.1007/s12040-017-0916-x)
second_source: Geen, Bordoni, Battisti, Hui (2020) Monsoons, ITCZs, and the concept of the global monsoon. Rev. Geophys. 58, e2020RG000700
note: The r value is from one paper. Kothawale & Rupa Kumar (2002) found the same sign (cited in Gadgil 2018 and Geen 2020 p.3-4).

claim: Gadgil's conclusion: the land-sea breeze view of the monsoon is not supported by observations of monsoon variability and 'abandoned'; the alternative is the monsoon as seasonal migration of the ITCZ/equatorial trough
value: land-sea breeze vs migrating convergence zone
source: Gadgil S. (2018) The monsoon system: Land-sea breeze or the ITCZ? J. Earth Syst. Sci. 127:1 (doi 10.1007/s12040-017-0916-x)
second_source: Geen, Bordoni, Battisti, Hui (2020) Monsoons, ITCZs, and the concept of the global monsoon. Rev. Geophys. 58, e2020RG000700
note: School texts (NCERT Class IX p.49, Class XI p.29, Class XI Fundamentals p.81) give land-sea heating as the cause. Gadgil (IISc) says abandon it; Geen et al. 2020 (independent group) say theory strongly supports the convergence-zone picture. Webster-style heating views persist in textbooks (Gadgil 2018 p.8 names Webster 1987, Lau & Li 1984). Teach: heating is the classic first idea; the current research view is the convergence zone; name the disagreement. Gemini found nothing new. Teaching decision stays with AK and the reviewer: classic heating view first, then the convergence-zone view, named as a disagreement. Gemini lead checked at source 2 Nov 2026 (VERIFY.md).

claim: Geen et al. (2020): monsoons historically seen as regional sea breezes; recent theory and observations support seeing them as localised seasonal migrations of the tropical convergence zone within a global monsoon; this is called a shift in understanding
source: Geen, Bordoni, Battisti, Hui (2020) Monsoons, ITCZs, and the concept of the global monsoon. Rev. Geophys. 58, e2020RG000700
second_source: Gadgil S. (2018) The monsoon system: Land-sea breeze or the ITCZ? J. Earth Syst. Sci. 127:1 (doi 10.1007/s12040-017-0916-x)
note: The same review says mountains, continent shapes and transient weather are not yet in the picture (abstract; section 5.2).

claim: Geen et al.: ITCZs are low-latitude (about 0-10 degrees poleward) convergence zones, monsoons about 10-25 degrees poleward; at Earth's rotation rate monsoon convergence zones appear unable to move beyond about 25 degrees from the equator
source: Geen, Bordoni, Battisti, Hui (2020) Monsoons, ITCZs, and the concept of the global monsoon. Rev. Geophys. 58, e2020RG000700
second_source: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch4 Climate (rev. ed. Feb 2022, reprint Mar 2026)
note: Matches NCERT Class XI p.34, which puts the July ITCZ near 25 N.

claim: NCERT: the ITCZ is a low-pressure zone at the equator where trade winds converge and air rises; in July it lies about 20-25 N over the Gangetic plain, called the monsoon trough; it encourages a thermal low over north and north-west India
source: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch4 Climate (rev. ed. Feb 2022, reprint Mar 2026)
second_source: Geen, Bordoni, Battisti, Hui (2020) Monsoons, ITCZs, and the concept of the global monsoon. Rev. Geophys. 58, e2020RG000700

claim: Over Indian longitudes there are two favoured cloud-band locations in summer, over the heated subcontinent and over the warm equatorial Indian Ocean; Gadgil therefore uses 'tropical convergence zone (TCZ)' rather than ITCZ
source: Gadgil S. (2003) The Indian monsoon and its variability. Annu. Rev. Earth Planet. Sci. 31:429-467 (doi 10.1146/annurev.earth.31.100901.141251)

claim: Heat low: a shallow low over the arid zone of north-west India, Pakistan and the Middle East in summer, reaching about 850 hPa (1.5 km) with a ridge above; much cloud but little rain
source: IMD Frequently Asked Questions on Monsoon (PDF created 16 Jul 2020)
second_source: Gadgil S. (2018) The monsoon system: Land-sea breeze or the ITCZ? J. Earth Syst. Sci. 127:1 (doi 10.1007/s12040-017-0916-x)
note: IMD FAQ links a deep heat low to a good monsoon and a weak one to 1987 drought; Gadgil 2018 says land temperature is lower in good years (different variables: pressure vs temperature).

claim: Monsoon trough: an elongated low-pressure area from the heat low over Pakistan to the head of the Bay of Bengal, a semi-permanent monsoon feature
source: IMD Frequently Asked Questions on Monsoon (PDF created 16 Jul 2020)
second_source: IMD Monsoon 2025: A Report (Met Monograph, issued 7 Apr 2026)

claim: Trough south of its normal position gives active/vigorous monsoon over most of India; trough moving north (to the Himalayan foothills) gives break conditions with heavy rain along the foothills and sometimes Brahmaputra floods
source: IMD Frequently Asked Questions on Monsoon (PDF created 16 Jul 2020)
second_source: IMD Monsoon 2025: A Report (Met Monograph, issued 7 Apr 2026)

source: IMD Frequently Asked Questions on Monsoon (PDF created 16 Jul 2020)
second_source: IMD Monsoon 2025: A Report (Met Monograph, issued 7 Apr 2026)
note: NCERT (p.30, 35) describes the same flow as south-east trades crossing the equator between 40 and 60 E but does not name the jet.

source: IMD CRS Research Report 3/2020, New Normal Dates of Onset/Progress and Withdrawal of SW Monsoon (Pai et al., 15 May 2020)
second_source: IMD Frequently Asked Questions on Monsoon (PDF created 16 Jul 2020)

source: IMD Monsoon 2025: A Report (Met Monograph, issued 7 Apr 2026)
second_source: IMD Frequently Asked Questions on Monsoon (PDF created 16 Jul 2020)

claim: Tropical Easterly Jet: upper-level (100-150 hPa) easterly jet near the latitude of Chennai from east Vietnam to west Africa; climatological speed 70-75 knots in July
source: IMD Monsoon 2025: A Report (Met Monograph, issued 7 Apr 2026)
second_source: IMD Frequently Asked Questions on Monsoon (PDF created 16 Jul 2020)
note: NCERT p.31 says the easterly jet sets in along 15 N.

claim: NCERT: the westerly jet stream withdraws from north India south of the Himalaya, then an easterly jet sets in along 15 N and is 'held responsible' for the burst of the monsoon
source: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch4 Climate (rev. ed. Feb 2022, reprint Mar 2026)
second_source: Ding 2007, J. Meteorol. Soc. Japan 85B:21-54 (review); Yanai, Li and Song 1992, JMSJ 70(1B)
note: No source read treats this as the cause. IMD's operational onset criteria use rainfall, westerly depth and OLR, not jets. Schiemann et al. (2009, ERA-40 1958-2001) put the median date of the westerly jet's move north of the Tibetan Plateau at 28 April, a month before Kerala onset. Yin (1949) and Koteswaram studies not read. Needs a review paper on jet and onset. Ding 2007 p.27: the easterly jet forms and the westerly jet jumps north as part of the onset circulation change; no open source says the jet shift causes the burst. Teach as things that happen together, never as the cause. Gemini lead checked at source 2 Nov 2026 (VERIFY.md).

claim: Tibetan High: warm upper-level anticyclone over the Tibetan Plateau in the monsoon, whose outflow feeds the Tropical Easterly Jet; IMD notes that westward shifts of the High would be 'against' it originating from plateau heating
source: IMD Frequently Asked Questions on Monsoon (PDF created 16 Jul 2020)
second_source: IMD Monsoon 2025: A Report (Met Monograph, issued 7 Apr 2026)
note: Centre quoted as 28 N 98 E (Q8) vs 25-28 N, 88-92 E in the 2025 report p.36: positions differ by level and month.

claim: Boos & Kuang (2010): in a model, removing the Tibetan Plateau but keeping the Himalaya and adjacent ranges leaves the large-scale South Asian monsoon circulation largely unchanged (plateau heating adds rain only along its southern edge); the mountains matter by insulating warm moist air over India from cold dry air to the north; peak upper-tropospheric temperature lies over India south of the plateau
source: Boos & Kuang (2010) Dominant control of the South Asian monsoon by orographic insulation versus plateau heating. Nature 463:218-222 (doi 10.1038/nature08707)
second_source: Boos and Kuang 2013 Sci. Rep. 3:1192; Wu et al. 2012 Sci. Rep. 2:404
note: IMD 2025 report p.36 and IMD research report RR 3/2020 p.6 describe the plateau as an elevated heat source that matters to the monsoon; Geen et al. 2020 p.21 reports the reinterpretation (mountains as a mechanical barrier). Boos & Kuang 2013 and Wu et al. 2012 (reported in searches, not read) continue the debate. Settled as a live debate: Boos and Kuang favour insulation; Wu et al. favour plateau heating for the north and east. Both reject the mountains-as-wall story. Teach as unsettled. Gemini lead checked at source 2 Nov 2026 (VERIFY.md).

second_source: Boos & Kuang (2010) Dominant control of the South Asian monsoon by orographic insulation versus plateau heating. Nature 463:218-222 (doi 10.1038/nature08707)
note: Consistent in spirit with Boos & Kuang 2010 (insulation from cold dry air).

claim: RBI MPC resolution (5-7 Oct 2026), para 6: deficient south-west monsoon and strong El Nino pose risks to the agriculture outlook and rural demand; foodgrain buffer expected to mitigate
value: risks to agriculture outlook and rural demand

claim: RBI MPC resolution (Oct 2026), para 9: near-term inflation outlook points to supply-side pressures from the deficient monsoon, El Nino, and high energy/commodity prices; CPI projected 5.2% for 2026-27
source: RBI, Resolution of the Monetary Policy Committee, October 5 to 7, 2026
note: Quote: "continued pressures from supply side on account of the deficient monsoon". Projection is RBI's, not an outcome.

claim: Kharif foodgrain production was 176.038 million tonnes of 376.563 Mt total (46.7%) in 2025-26 (3rd Advance Estimates); 2024-25 kharif 169.460 of 357.732 Mt (47.4%)
source: Dept of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare, Third Advance Estimate of Production of Food Grains 2025-26 (as on 27.05.2026)
page_or_section: Page 2, row 19 Total Food Grains: Kharif 1760.38, Rabi 1805.12, Summer 200.13, Total 3765.63 lakh tonnes
second_source: PIB release 27 May 2026 gives total 376.563 Mt
note: Share is our arithmetic (1760.38/3765.63). Kharif+rabi+summer = total. Advance estimate, not final; kharif is the monsoon-sown crop, rabi is not mainly monsoon rain.

claim: Economic Survey 2025-26 para 5.37: above-normal monsoon in 2025 augmented reservoir levels, favourably influenced kharif harvests and improved foodgrain stocks; likely to keep food inflation moderate
source: Ministry of Finance, Economic Survey 2025-26, Ch. 5 Inflation
note: Quote: "above-normal monsoon, which augmented reservoir levels, has favorably influenced kharif harvests". Refers to 2025 monsoon.

claim: Economic Survey 2025-26 para 1.17: agricultural activity in H1 FY26 was supported by a favourable monsoon; agricultural GVA grew 3.6% (H1 FY25: 2.7%), below long-term average 4.5%
source: Ministry of Finance, Economic Survey 2025-26, Ch. 1 State of the Economy
second_source: Same Survey, Ch. 6 para 6.9 (production increase attributed to favourable monsoon)
note: Survey adds that crop growth is variable with limited productivity gains, so rain is not the whole story.
